# gapwise

gapwise is an R package for data in which the same units are measured more
than once: patients at follow-up visits, hospitals by month, countries by
year. It finds the observations that are missing from such data, makes them
visible, and creates lagged variables that stay correct when observations are
missing.

## The problem it solves

Suppose two patients were each meant to attend four visits.

| patient | visit | blood pressure |
|---------|-------|----------------|
| A       | 1     | 120            |
| A       | 2     | 125            |
| A       | 3     | 130            |
| A       | 4     | 128            |
| B       | 1     | 140            |
| B       | 2     | 138            |
| B       | 4     | 150            |

Patient B did not attend visit 3, so the table simply has one row fewer.
Nothing in the data says that an observation is missing. In a file with
thousands of rows this goes unnoticed, and it causes two kinds of error.

1. **Missing data are undercounted.** Counting `NA` values finds none, even
   though one of eight planned measurements was never taken.
2. **Lagged variables are wrong.** Many analyses use the value from the
   previous time point. The usual code takes the value from the row above.
   For patient B at visit 4, the row above is visit 2, so 138 is recorded as
   the previous blood pressure. The true previous value, at visit 3, is
   unknown.

gapwise has one function for each step of dealing with this.

| Function         | What it does                                                        |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `check_panel()`  | Reports duplicated rows, absent rows, and whether the data are complete |
| `fill_panel()`   | Adds the absent rows, with `NA` for the values that were not measured |
| `add_lag()`      | Adds a lagged variable matched on the time value, not the row above  |
| `miss_by_time()` | Counts missing values for each variable at each time point           |
| `plot_missing()` | Draws which units are missing a variable at which time points        |
| `attrition()`    | Counts how many units are still observed at each time point          |

## Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Jimmuji/gapwise")
```

Then load it:

```{r}
library(gapwise)
```

## How to call the functions

Every function takes the data first, then the names of two columns, in
quotes:

* `id` is the column that says which unit a row belongs to.
* `time` is the column that says which time point a row belongs to.

The data must be in long format, meaning one row per unit and time point.

## Example data

Two data sets come with the package, so every example below runs as shown.

* `visits` is a simulated cohort of 60 patients who were each meant to attend
  5 visits. Some patients drop out, some skip a visit, and some measurements
  were not recorded.
* `conflict` has one row per country and year for 186 countries from 2000 to
  2019, with armed conflict and mortality indicators.

```{r}
head(visits)
```

## A worked example

### 1. Check the structure

```{r}
result <- check_panel(visits, id = "patient", time = "visit")
result
```

Sixty patients and five visits should give 300 rows, but there are 240.
Of the 60 absent rows, 9 are gaps (the patient came back later) and 51 fall
after the patient's last visit.

The absent rows are listed in `result$absent`:

```{r}
head(result$absent)
```

By default the expected time points are the ones that appear somewhere in
the data. If you know what they should be, pass them in `times`, for example
`times = 1:5`. This also catches a time point that every unit is missing.

### 2. Make the absent rows visible

```{r}
filled <- fill_panel(visits, id = "patient", time = "visit", constant = "sex")
nrow(filled)
filled[filled$patient == "P002", ]
```

Patient P002 now has a row for visit 3 with `NA` measurements. Columns
listed in `constant` do not change within a unit, so they are copied into
the new row instead of being left empty.

### 3. Lag a variable safely

Here is the row-above approach applied to patient P002, followed by
`add_lag()`.

```{r}
p002 <- visits[visits$patient == "P002", c("patient", "visit", "sbp")]

# the row above: wrong at visit 4
p002$row_above <- c(NA, head(p002$sbp, -1))

# matched on the visit number: correct
p002 <- add_lag(p002, var = "sbp", id = "patient", time = "visit")
p002
```

At visit 4 the row-above column reports 127, which was measured at visit 2.
`add_lag()` looks for visit 3, finds no row, and returns `NA`.

`add_lag()` works within each unit, so a value is never carried from the end
of one unit to the start of the next. The rows do not need to be sorted, and
they are returned in their original order. Use `n` for longer lags, for
example `n = 2`.

### 4. See where values are missing

`miss_by_time()` separates the two reasons a value can be missing: the unit
has no row at that time point (`n_absent`), or the row is there but the
value is `NA` (`n_na`).

```{r}
miss_by_time(visits, id = "patient", time = "visit", vars = "sbp")
```

Counting `NA` values in the original data would report `r sum(is.na(visits$sbp))`
missing blood pressure readings. The true number is
`r sum(miss_by_time(visits, "patient", "visit", vars = "sbp")$n_missing)`.

`plot_missing()` shows the same information for each patient.

```{r plot-missing, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 8, fig.alt = "Tile plot of 60 patients by 5 visits. Most tiles are blue for observed. Green tiles for absent rows build up toward later visits, and a few orange tiles mark values that were not recorded."}
plot_missing(visits, var = "sbp", id = "patient", time = "visit")
```

### 5. Count who is still in the study

```{r}
attrition(visits, id = "patient", time = "visit")
```

`n_dropped_after` is the number of patients seen at that visit and never
again. Add `var = "sbp"` to count a patient as observed only when blood
pressure was actually recorded.

## The same functions on country data

Nothing in the package is specific to patients. With `conflict`, the unit is
the country and the time point is the year.

```{r}
check_panel(conflict, id = "iso", time = "year")
```

No rows are absent, but that does not mean no values are missing:

```{r}
mm <- miss_by_time(conflict, id = "iso", time = "year", vars = "matmor")
tail(mm, 4)
```

The maternal mortality ratio is missing for all 186 countries in 2018 and
2019, which shortens any analysis of it by two years.

A lagged exposure, here armed conflict in the previous year:

```{r}
lagged <- add_lag(conflict, var = "armedconflict", id = "iso", time = "year")
head(lagged[, c("iso", "year", "armedconflict", "armedconflict_lag1")], 3)
```

## Getting help

Every function and both data sets have a help page with examples:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?check_panel
?add_lag
help(package = "gapwise")
```

If a function stops with an error about duplicated rows or missing values in
`id` or `time`, run `check_panel()` first. It reports those problems instead
of stopping.
